Meeting header: 2026-04-29 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Arun (Redwood SA), Priya (Helion VP Eng), Marco (Helion Infra), Eva (Helion SRE), Samir (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Focus on why Helion sees occasional p99 spikes during streaming inference when crossing VPC edge, discuss KV cache hotkeying and how batching interacts with short sequence workloads, evaluate quantization choices for cost/latency.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya (Helion): Priya here.
[00:07] Marco: Marco.
[00:08] Eva: Eva.
[00:09] Samir: Samir on the ML infra side.
[00:12] Jonah (Redwood SE): Jonah, thanks all. We'll jump into the traces Priya sent, and then walk through streaming vs non-streaming experiments.

[02:05] Jonah: So first thing I want to call out — the traces show two classes of spikes. One looks like KV cache miss amplification, and the other looks like networking microbursts at the VPC edge when requests hit a cold path and then fall back to a larger model.
[02:28] Marco: When you say "KV cash miss" — sorry, "KV cache miss" — do you mean our prefix cache not populated for user sessions? We do TTLs of 10 minutes, but sessions are short.
[02:37] Jonah: Right, we're seeing a mix. A lot of short sessions with small prompts means prefix diversity; KV cache hit rate drops and then you get serialization + deserialization plus a network round trip to the shard. That combined with streaming chunking adds jitter.

[04:14] Priya: We're mostly using streaming for the UX; lower user-perceived latency. But the SREs keep seeing those 500–700 ms p99 spikes even though median is great.
[04:27] Eva: Yeah, median 40 ms, but p99 jumps to 650–800 ms on certain windows. It's inconsistent which is what's maddening.

[05:10] Jonah: Two quick hypotheses: 1) network hops — your VPC edge to our private subnets adds variable latency; 2) continuous batching + streaming interaction — when a stream is triggered it holds the request open and batching decisions can delay a chunk if batch window misaligns.

[06:02] Arun (Redwood SA): Also quantization can change per-token compute time, especially with mixed-int8 fallback. Some chips spike when a kernel triggers a fallback path for certain layers.
[06:18] Samir: Can you expand on the fallback path? Our runs used 4-bit quant on some models — we saw slight quality diffs but expected speed ups.
[06:28] Jonah: With aggressive quant (like Q4 or similar) the runtime sometimes switches kernels for specific ops which are slower on certain GPU architectures; that leads to uneven per-token timing across long sequences, which shows up at p95/p99.

[07:55] Maya: Let's pause and map the end-to-end: client -> VPC edge -> load balancer -> Redwood node (streaming handler) -> KV shard (may be remote) -> model worker(s). Each arrow is a potential variable.
[08:12] Marco: In our topology we have a VPC peering plus NAT at the edge for egress constraints. Could NAT connection reuse or SNAT table limits cause bursts?
[08:25] Jonah: Yes. SNAT exhaustion or ephemeral port churn can introduce retries and timeouts if connection reuse isn't configured. We sometimes see that in high-concurrency short requests.

[10:00] Priya: For our landing page feature it's literally thousands of 80–150 token prompts per minute with a lot of unique prefixes. So KV hit rate is only ~32% in some hours.
[10:15] Jonah: That matches the heatmap Marcus (Redwood) saw in the sample. We recommend two immediate mitigations: bump KV TTL for sessions that are sticky, and introduce a small local LRU prefetch on the streaming handler to catch top-200 keys.
[10:39] Marco: Local LRU prefetch — would that increase memory on each node? We have strict memory profiles on our edge infra.
[10:46] Arun: Minimal; prefetching only top-200 keys per node is typically a few MBs depending on key size, but it reduces cross-shard RTTs significantly for common prefixes.

[12:05] Eva: What's the tradeoff with batching? We were under impression batching always reduces p99 because of better GPU utilization. But in our case streaming seems worse at tail.
[12:18] Jonah: Two things: naive batching increases latency — you wait for batch window; but smart continuous batching tries to fill batches without exceeding latency SLOs. With streaming, each emitted chunk might be gated by batching decisions which can add jitter if the batch windows aren't aligned with chunk boundaries.
[12:42] Jonah: Example: if you use 20 ms batch window, and streaming emits every 15 ms, some chunks cross windows and get held for additional 20 ms. That shows up as high p95 for chunks, not full responses.

[14:10] Samir: Could we set per-route batching windows? For the landing page route we can tolerate median steady state but want tighter worst-case.
[14:19] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports per-route batching configs. You can set max-latency per route and a min batch size. Route-level pinning to dedicated worker pools also helps reduce cross-customer noise.

[16:00] Priya: About on-prem — if we move the model workers into our own racks, would that eliminate the VPC edge spikes?
[16:10] Jonah: It would remove the public VPC hop but you'd still see intra-datacenter network jitter and KV shard placement effects. On-prem gives you control over NIC settings, jumbo frames, and consistent LAN latencies, but you must provision KV redundancy and fast interconnects.
[16:40] Marco: We actually have an RDMA-capable fabric. Could Redwood runtime leverage that?
[16:48] Arun: We have experimental RDMA paths for KV replication in Private deployments; we should run a lab test. That usually drops p99 by 20–40% for KV-heavy workloads.

[18:12] Eva: Any thoughts on fallback policies? Sometimes the system falls back to a larger model during congestion and that causes giant spikes.
[18:23] Jonah: Right — our standard fallback flow is 'try-fast-variant -> if error or SLO breach then route to larger model'. That can increase latency if the larger model is cold. We recommend canary warming and pre-warmed standby capacity for critical routes.

[20:00] Marco: Do you have metrics for warming hit improvements?
[20:05] Arun: In our internal tests, pre-warmed standby reduced p99 of fallback events from 1.2s to ~280ms because the target model had its KV and kernels in warm caches and GPU memory.

[22:37] Priya: Let's talk quantization again: we tried Q4 and Q8, and Q4 gave small perf wins but occasional outliers. Is there a recommended hybrid?
[22:50] Jonah: Hybrid profiles often give the best p95/p99. For critical layers that are sensitive, you keep them in higher-precision and quantize the rest. Redwood Optimize can suggest a per-layer profile based on your eval set. We'll run that against your sample prompts.

[25:12] Samir: Is there a quick test we can run to surface kernel fallback path issues on our infra?
[25:18] Jonah: Yes — run a sustained token-generation trace at varying sequence lengths and inspect per-layer latency histograms. If certain ops have heavy tail, that's the candidate for higher-precision pinning. We'll provide a script.

[27:44] Maya: Quick note about monitoring — enable per-token tracing and route-level tracing in the console, that'll surface whether spikes happen pre-model (network/KV) or in-model.

[29:30] Marco: We also observed TCP retransmits in some windows. Could that be due to our SNAT or our firewall inspection?
[29:40] Jonah: Possibly; FW inspection can cause pause if it's inline. We recommend bypassing deep inspection for intra-VPC traffic or permit long-lived connections for the streaming handlers.

[31:10] Priya: In terms of an immediate pilot, we want: 1) Redwood to run streaming vs non-streaming tests with our traces, 2) a workshop on our VPC/NAT config, 3) a quantization profile run.
[31:25] Maya: Agreed. We'll schedule the VPC workshop with our infra folks. Jonah, you'll own the bench runs.

[33:00] Jonah: I'll run both modes: pure streaming, streaming with micro-batching, and non-streaming (batch-return) with identical workload, and we'll capture p50/p95/p99 per chunk and per full response. Expect CSV output and a short writeup.

[35:08] Samir: For the KV hotkey list, will you need key sizes? We have variable-sized context payloads.
[35:15] Jonah: Yes — please include average key size and serialized payload distribution. That affects memory and prefetch decisions.

[37:00] Eva: Any immediate config change we can flip that won't impact quality?
[37:05] Arun: Increase the route-level max in-flight requests and pin routing to fewer nodes to reduce cross-shard network hops. Also enable local LRU for top keys if memory allows.

[39:10] Marco: Are there any known bugs that produce outliers during streaming?
[39:14] Jonah: There's an older scheduling bug on kernels on a specific driver version that can cause one-in-a-thousand slow tokens; we've got a fix but will confirm if your runtime sees it. We'll check driver / CUDA versions during the network workshop.

[41:30] Priya: Let's capture expected numbers: our SLO is p95 < 200 ms and p99 < 350 ms for first-token-latency on the landing route.
[41:44] Maya: Noted. Based on initial trace, median is okay but p99 is off. Our aim is to get p99 under 350 ms with recommended mitigations (prefetch, route pinning, pre-warm).

[44:00] Jonah: I'll also run an experiment where we intentionally increase batching window and show how p50 improves but p99 regresses for streams — useful to pick the right knob.

[46:12] Samir: If we switch to non-streaming for the landing page, will user-perceived latency actually get worse?
[46:20] Jonah: Not necessarily. For short responses, non-streaming (single-shot) can match streaming perceived latency because you avoid chunk boundary jitter. For longer streaming outputs, streaming is still better for UX. We should run both and do A/B.

[48:35] Priya: About security and on-prem: we need to see the private deployment network diagram and KMS integration.
[48:43] Maya: I'll share the Private deployment architecture & KMS guide in the next 24 hours. It's in our secure docs repo; I'll include the access link.

[51:00] Marco: Could Redwood run a synthetic test that simulates our SNAT exhaustion pattern?
[51:06] Jonah: Yes — we'll create a test that opens many short-lived outbound connections to replicate ephemeral port churn and show mitigation by connection reuse or pooling.

[53:30] Eva: Any reason not to bump KV TTL aggressively?
[53:34] Arun: Main tradeoff is staleness for user-specific prefixes. For generative tasks TTL increases can help for cold keys, but for per-user dynamic context you may serve stale prefixes. We often recommend selective TTL increase only for non-sensitive or globally popular prefixes.

[55:12] Priya: OK let's recap next steps.
[55:20] Maya: Recap: Redwood will (1) run streaming vs non-streaming bench with Helion traces (Jonah), (2) share quantization per-layer suggestions & cost delta (Arun), (3) send Private/VPC design & KMS docs (Maya), (4) schedule VPC & driver workshop (Maya/Jonah). Helion will (1) provide KV hotkey export and sample traces (Marco), (2) confirm pilot stakeholders (Priya).

[56:05] Marco: Timeline? We need initial bench results for exec review next Tuesday.
[56:11] Jonah: We can have the first bench CSV and short writeup by 2026-05-07; quick win configs and the VPC workshop week of May 5th.

[58:40] Priya: Thanks, this was useful. If we can hit p99 under 350 ms with small config changes that'll make the feature viable.
[58:50] Maya: We'll prioritize. I'll put the links and notes in the follow-up.
[59:02] Samir: One last micro-note — please include per-layer tails in the bench output so we can pin problem layers quickly.
[59:10] Jonah: Yup — per-layer histograms included.
[60:00] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs. Meeting adjourned.
